Ada wanted to deliver a library book to Nell, who hoped for quiet in the square. Bram’s cart was damaged, and its cover was loose; even the breeze seemed ready to make matters worse. Mayor Bell’s promised biggest parade suddenly had a very wobbly beginning.

Ada noticed Nell watching the noisy preparations. “I hope Nell wants quiet,” Ada whispered. Nell nodded. That was the exact thing she wanted. Bram checked his cart and found the damage: one wheel wobbled, and the cart gave a sadly lopsided creak. “You are not ready,” he told it. The cart seemed to agree. Ada told Mayor Bell, “Nell wants quiet.” Mayor Bell lowered the parade horn from his lips. “Quiet?” he said. “That is a very small sound—and perhaps a very important one.”

Bram tightened the loose wheel and tested the cart with a careful push. This time it rolled straight. “Ready,” he announced. “Now you can carry something more useful than my lunch.”

Ada noticed the breeze tugging ribbons in the square. “That wind is breezy,” she said, watching a scrap of paper scoot past like it had somewhere important to be. Ada told Bram about the breeze. Bram looked at the cart’s loose cover. “Then the wind may borrow the cover,” he said, “unless I tie it down first.”

Bram tied the cart’s loose cover firmly. He tugged the knot twice. The cover stayed put, even when the breeze gave it a testing flap.

Bram lent Ada the cart after securing its cover. “Now the wind can fuss all it likes,” he said. “It may flap, but it may not fly away with our cargo.” Ada took Bram’s borrowed cart from the workshop to the library, where the book waited. Its wheels bumped over the floorboards with a polite little clop-clop. With the book tucked safely aboard, Ada rolled Bram’s cart from the library to the town square. She kept both hands on the handle and steered around every pebble.

Ada delivered the book to Nell beneath the tied cover. The breeze rustled above them, but the pages stayed safe. Nell accepted the book with a grateful smile.

Mayor Bell saw that the book now belonged to Nell. He looked at the book, then at his enormous horn, as if the horn had suddenly grown rather silly.

Mayor Bell led a quiet book procession. No drum boomed; no horn blared. He walked proudly while Nell held her book, and the whole parade made only the soft shush of shoes.

The breeze danced around the square, lifting ribbons but not the cart’s tied cover. Under it, Nell held her book safely while Mayor Bell led a proud, quiet procession. The cart’s knots made tiny taps in the wind, like two little drumbeats keeping everyone calm.

Ada wanted to deliver a library book to Nell in the square, but Bram’s cart was damaged. Its wheel pointed one way while the cart pointed another—rather like a duck giving directions. Nell wanted to join Mayor Bell’s enormous parade, which had not yet made room for her.

Bram checked his cart and found the damage: one wheel wobbled, and the cart gave a sadly lopsided creak. “You are not ready,” he told it. The cart seemed to agree. Ada noticed Nell peering toward the parade preparations. “I want to join,” Nell said. Ada heard her clearly and remembered the exact wish.

Bram tightened the loose wheel and tested the cart with a careful push. This time it rolled straight. “Ready,” he announced. “Now you can carry something more useful than my lunch.”

Bram rested one hand on the cart. “It is ready, and the square is still. You may borrow it, Ada—but roll gently. It is a cart, not a galloping goat.” Ada took Bram’s borrowed cart from the workshop to the library, where the book waited. Its wheels bumped over the floorboards with a polite little clop-clop. With the book tucked safely aboard, Ada rolled Bram’s cart from the library to the town square. She kept both hands on the handle and steered around every pebble. Ada told Mayor Bell, “Nell wants to join.” Mayor Bell blinked. His parade had been designed for spectators, not a book-holding helper. “Then we shall make room,” he said.

Ada handed the book to Nell at the square. Nell held it against her chest. “Now I can join the parade,” she said, looking delighted rather than book-buried.

Mayor Bell saw that the book now belonged to Nell. He looked at the book, then at his enormous horn, as if the horn had suddenly grown rather silly.

Mayor Bell welcomed Nell into the parade with a cheerful wave. Nell joined while holding her book, and Mayor Bell cheered—not for the size of his parade, but for the newest person in it.

The parade rolled on with Nell at its heart, her new book held high like a bright little flag. Mayor Bell cheered, Ada grinned, and Bram’s cart carried its borrowed treasure steadily. What began as one grand parade now had one more happy marcher than anyone had planned.

Ada wanted to invite Mira to Frog’s pond concert, and Ben wanted to help. Yet Mira wanted quiet while a breeze skimmed the pond, and Ada’s wide lily pad still waited in the garden. Frog’s acorn drum waited too, although it belonged to Frog and not to Ada.

Frog carried his acorn drum from the garden to the pond. He set it near the water, where its round wooden belly was ready to go bonk—or perhaps merely bonk politely.

Ada picked up the painted invitation and carried it from the garden to the porch. She held it carefully; the blue frog on its front had very important-looking spots.

With the invitation waiting on the porch, Ada walked up from the garden. She practiced her polite knock, then decided one knock was plenty.

Ada peeked toward Mira’s porch and noticed Mira sitting with a book, enjoying quiet. “Quiet,” Ada whispered, “is Mira’s wish today.”

Ada gave Mira the painted invitation. “A pond concert,” she said, “with a very small volume knob.” Mira accepted it from Ada with a curious smile.

Ada told Frog, “Mira wants quiet today.” Frog nodded. “Then my drum shall use its teeny-tiniest toes.”

Knowing Mira wanted quiet, Frog played a gentle song on the acorn drum. Tap, hush, tap—each note skimmed the pond like a tiny pebble that had learned manners.

The invitation was safely delivered: Mira now owned the painted card, and Ada’s delivery was complete. The blue frog on the card seemed pleased with its new address.

Mira smiled and listened to Frog’s gentle pond song. She stayed on the porch, quiet as a sleeping feather, while the soft taps reached her.

Mira smiled and listened as Frog’s gentle notes floated across the still pond. Ada’s invitation rested safely in Mira’s hands, and the acorn drum made no thunder at all. In the evening light, each quiet ripple looked like a little silver ear, listening too.

Ada planned to invite Mira to Frog’s pond concert, while Ben hoped to help. Mira wanted to join, but the pond was perfectly still and the concert tools were scattered in the garden. Ada’s painted invitation waited beside a wide lily pad, as if both were awaiting instructions.

Ada picked up the painted invitation and carried it from the garden to the porch. She held it carefully; the blue frog on its front had very important-looking spots.

Ada pushed her wide lily pad from the garden onto the pond. It floated broad and steady, making a perfect little platform for Frog’s planned rhythm. Ada watched Mira on the porch, where Mira leaned forward as though eager for music. “She wants to join,” Ada observed. “That is wonderfully less quiet than a potato.” Ada told Frog that Mira wanted to join the concert. Frog puffed up happily. “Excellent! I know three rhythms and one accidental sneeze.”

Frog began a lively rhythm on the lily pad. The still pond let every plip and plop travel outward, while the pad bobbed like a cheerful green drumhead.

Mira joined the lively pond rhythm from the porch, tapping along with her fingers. Her smile arrived on the beat, though her left thumb was slightly ahead of everyone.
